body.p: I. Introduction

Claims 1-17 are pending in the present application. No new matter has been added. This paper is being filed with a request for consideration under the After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP) program to consider amendments made to simplify the issues by rendering all rejections moot. In view of the foregoing amendments and the following remarks, it is respectfully submitted that all the pending claims are allowable, and reconsideration is respectfully requested.
II. Rejection of Claim 14 Under 35 U.S.C. k 112 - Written Description

Claim 14 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112 as to written description. Claim 14 satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112, and the rejection should be withdrawn, for at least the following reasons.
The Office Action asserts that claim 14 introduces new matter because it introduces the term "ego vehicle," which term does not appear in the originally filed application.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the merits of this rejection because there is no requirement for the specification to describe the features of the claims using the exact terms used in the claims. As stated by the Board in Exparte Sorenson, 3 U.S.P.Q. 2d 1462, 1463 (Bd. Pat. App. Int. 1987) (emphasis added):
[W]e are mindful that appellant's specification need not describe the claimed invention in ipsis verbis to comply with the written description requirement.
The test is whether the originally filed specification disclosure reasonably conveys to a person having ordinary skill that applicant had possession of
the subject matter later claimed. ...

In particular, the Sorenson Board, noting that the examiner only essentially stated that the claim expressions at issue did not "appear in the original disclosure," found that the examiner had not met his initial burden of "presenting evidence why a person having ordinary skill in the art would not recognize in appellant's specification a description of the invention defined by the claims" - and that the "only reasoning presented" that the Board could discern was an "example of ipse dixit reasoning, resting on a bare assertion by the Examiner."

In this regard, in the context of patent applications (and more broadly, the automotive industry), an "ego vehicle" refers to the vehicle whose perspective is being considered in a particular system or scenario. It is the vehicle that the system is actively controlling or monitoring, and relative to the position and movement of which the environment is perceived. The meaning is established through its consistent use in technical literature and patent applications related to driving and related technologies. The definition of the term is implicit from the many publications and patents focusing on driving systems that describe path planning, object detection and avoidance and other vehicle-related publications, in which the ego vehicle is the vehicle (a) from whose perspective the surroundings are sensed, and

(b) whose maneuvers are accordingly controlled. Indeed, searching patent databases for "ego vehicle" along with terms like "autonomous driving," "path planning," or "sensor fusion" will reveal numerous examples. In other words, the term "ego vehicle" is a term that is well understood in the art, especially of automotive and related technologies to have the meaning discussed.

The present application describes how a first vehicle detects maneuvers of another vehicle that is leading the first vehicle; thereby surmises a state of objects in the surroundings, which objects are not directly visible to the first vehicle; and responsively executes a measure. Since the first vehicle is described as making the detections and responsively executing a measure, the first vehicle of the application is clearly an "ego vehicle" as the term is commonly used in the relevant art.

Therefore, like that which is discussed in Ex parte Sorenson, here as well, although the text of the claims and specification might not be exactly the same and the specification does not use the specific term "ego" that is recited claim 14, the specification clearly describes and provides written description support for this term of the claims. Since one of ordinary skill in the art would readily recognize that the application provides support for the recited term, therefore the only basis for this rejection is improper ipse dixit reasoning based on an improper ipsis verbis requirement.

Notwithstanding Applicant's disagreement, claim 14 is amended herein without prejudice to refer to a first vehicle instead of an ego vehicle, as this does not change the meaning of the claim substantively.
Withdrawal of the written description of claim 14 is therefore respectfully requested.
III. Rejection of Claim 14 Under 35 U.S.C. 112 - Definiteness

Claim 14 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112 as to definiteness. The rejection is due to an error in claim 14, which has been corrected herein by an amendment to claim 14. Withdrawal of the definiteness rejection of claim 14 is therefore respectfully requested.
IV. Rejection of Claims 1 and 7-13 Under 35 U.S.C. 4 102

Claims 1 and 7-13 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as anticipated by U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2013/0018526 ("Kelly"). Kelly does not anticipate any of the present claims, and the rejection should be withdrawn, for at least the following reasons.

The claims are allowable for the reasons already explained in the response previously filed on July 29, 2024. Specifically, Applicant previously explained that independent claims 1, 12, and 13 are directed to a first vehicle (this is an ego vehicle) detecting information about a leading vehicle (second vehicle), by which the first vehicle determines a maneuver performed by the leading vehicle or that the leading vehicle has driven over an obstacle. The first vehicle then uses that information regarding the leading vehicle to detect the obstacle itself. Kelly does not suggest these features of an indirect detection of an obstacle by using a detection about a leading vehicle in order to detect the obstacle.

Kelly describes a special system used for developing a crash avoidance system of a subject vehicle 650. Kelly's subject vehicle 650 is the ego vehicle, which is relied upon as corresponding to the first vehicle of the claims. The special system takes the forn of a dynamic motion element (DME) 100 which is a very low profile self-driving system that the ego/host/first vehicle 650 can drive over. The DME 100 is placed under a soft vehicle 600, referred to as a guided soft target (GST). This appears to essentially be a blow-up toy of typical car size that rides on top of the DME 100. The purpose of this combined system 100/600 is for it to simulate scenarios of a real-world vehicle while the ego/host/first vehicle 650 drives behind the simulation vehicle 100/600 (which is therefore relied upon as corresponding to the second vehicle of the claims). Figs. 6A-6D show the ego/host/first vehicle 650 driving and crashing into the combined system/second vehicle 100/600. (Kelly also describes a similar system for simulating a pedestrian as shown in Fig. 7, where a soft mannequin 700 is placed on top of the DME 100.)

The Office Action cites to pars. 2, 34, 45, and 58 of Kelly, as well as Figs. 6C-6D. Par. 2 states that the ego/host/first vehicle 650 can detect its surroundings using various sensors. Par. 34 discloses using those sensors to detect presence of an obstacle in front

of the ego/host/first vehicle 650, in order to perform a reactionary action in case an obstacle is detected with which the ego/host/first vehicle 650 determines it is likely to collide. Par. 34 states that some of these sensor systems are so sensitive that they may take a reactionary action even when detecting the low profile DME 100. But this is not desirable. In other words, when performing testing, we do not want the DME 100 to be treated as an obstacle. Therefore, par. 34 states that it is important to minimize an extent to which the DME 100 contributes to a detected radar (or other sensor) signature. Therefore, this section is describing ensuring that the DME 100 is not detected by the ego/host/first vehicle 650.

Par. 45 generally lists functions that the DME 100 can perform, including guidance/navigation and "data input and output," where inputs can include GOS information, compass information, and yaw rate information.

Par. 58 describes a use case of the simulation vehicle/second vehicle 100/600 forming a guided soft target system (GST) 800 to evaluate a collision mitigation system (A- CMBS) of the ego/host/first vehicle 650 which is supposed to take a reactionary action to a case in which, when properly functioning, the A-CMBS should detect that a collision is likely.
Thus, none of those cited sections suggest an indirect obstacle detection by the ego-first vehicle to which the present claims are directed.

In the "Response to Arguments" section, the Office Action makes a number of points. First the Office Action asserts that the description of claims 1, 12, and 13 as including the feature of an indirect obstacle detection is not in the claims. Second, the "ego" vehicle mentioned in the argument would, if recited in the claims, be considered to be new matter anyway. Third, par. 34 of Kelly discloses the feature that is actually recited in the claims. However, the Office Action is incorrect on all three points.

Contrary to the Office's assertion, if the term "ego" vehicle would be present in the claims, this would not constitute new matter for the reasons already explained above. Moreover, that claims 1, 12, and 13 do not actually include the term "ego" vehicle is not relevant. When the presented argument referred to an "ego" vehicle, this was simply a reference to the "first" vehicle which is recited in the claims. The claims refer to the first vehicle as recording information concerning the second vehicle, refer to a computer of the first vehicle detecting a maneuver of the second vehicle based on that recorded information, which detection is used to further detect an obstacle. Thus, the claims refer to actions from the perspective of the first vehicle, the first vehicle therefore properly being referred to as the ego vehicle.

Additionally, contrary to the Office's assertion, claims 1, 12, and 13 clearly refer to where an indirect obstacle detection is made by the first vehicle. In this regard, the claims provide that the first vehicle records information about a second-leading vehicle by which a maneuver of that second vehicle is detected by the first vehicle. The claims further recite that the obstacle is then detected depending on that detected maneuver of the second vehicle. This is an indirect detection of the obstacle, where the obstacle is detected due to the detection of the second-leading vehicle's maneuver.

Finally, par. 34 of Kelly does not disclose this feature. Further in this regard, the Office Action asserts that the reason par. 34 is considered the discussed feature of the claims is because in par. 34 "Kelly uses radar to detect a second vehicle (subject vehicle 650) to alert a driver to take evasive action, and avoid a collision." While it is true that par. 34 describes alerting a driver of a vehicle or the vehicle taking an evasive action if an object with which the vehicle is likely to collide is detected, this does not suggest anything different than a first vehicle directly detecting presence of an object and performing a responsive warning or maneuver. This does not suggest a first vehicle detecting a maneuver of a second vehicle, and then using this detection of the maneuver of the second vehicle to detect the obstacle.
Notwithstanding Applicant's disagreement with the rejection for these reasons, to facilitate matters, claims 1, 12, and 13 have been amended herein without prejudice for additional clarity.
Kelly therefore does not disclose or suggest all of the features of 1, 12, and 13 and therefore does not anticipate any of claims 1, 12, and 13 or any of claims 7-11, which depend from claim 1.
Withdrawal of the anticipation rejection of claims 1 and 7-13 is therefore respectfully requested.
V. Rejection of Claims 2 and 4 Under 35 U.S.C. # 103

Claims 2 and 4 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2020/0255013 ("Lee"). Claims 2 and 4 depend from claim I and are therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Lee merely generally describes sensors that an ego/host vehicle can use to detect presence, location, speed, direction, and type of a surrounding vehicle and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claims 2 and 4 is therefore respectfully requested.
VI. Rejection of Claim 3 Under 35 U.S.C. 103

Claim 3 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly, Lee, and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2005/0169530 ("Nakai"). Claim 3 depends from claim 2 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 2 because Nakai merely describes detections by an ego/host vehicle of measurements directly of the obstacle itself based on relationships between image data captured by two different cameras of the ego/host vehicle and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly and Lee noted above as to claim 2. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 3 is therefore respectfully requested.
VII. Rejection of Claim 5 Under 35 U.S.C. 4 103

Claim 5 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2021/0129750 ("Nugent"). Claim 5 depends from claim 1 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Nugent merely describes detections by an ego/host vehicle of measurements directly of the obstacle itself and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 5 is therefore respectfully requested.
VIII. Rejection of Claim 6 Under 35 U.S.C. 4 103

Claim 6 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as unpatentable over the combination of Kelly and U.S. Pat. App. Pub. No. 2010/0013615 ("Hebert"). Claim 6 depends from claim 1 and is therefore allowable for at least the same reasons as claim 1 because Hebert merely states that an ego/host vehicle can perform a guidance to avoid obstacles and does not correct the critical deficiencies of Kelly noted above as to claim 1. Withdrawal of the obviousness rejection of claim 6 is therefore respectfully requested.
IX. Conclusion

All issues raised having been addressed, it is therefore respectfully requested that the rejections be withdrawn. Prompt reconsideration and allowance of the present application are therefore earnestly solicited.
